meta.title: Hearing the One Note
meta.summary: Train the ear on the note that moves rather than on the chord's mood, then put a minor triad into a progression on strings 1-2-3 that never leaves the first five frets.

spans.text: You can build every grip in this chapter and still not hear which one you are playing. That is a separate skill, and the usual advice for it — major sounds happy, minor sounds sad — is a poor place to start, because it asks your ear for a feeling instead of a fact.
Two problems with mood as a listening target. The first is that it is at least partly

rather than acoustic: the happy/sad association is strong and early in listeners raised on Western music, and much weaker as a universal than it is usually presented. The second is more practical — it falls apart in real music. A minor chord in the right spot sounds bright and lifting; a major chord in the wrong one sounds wistful. The mood belongs to the passage, not to the chord.

What is reliably there every single time is the note. The root is the same, the fifth is the same, and the third sits three semitones above the root instead of four. That is the entire acoustic difference between the two chords, and it is what your ear should be reaching for.

In root position the third is the middle note — the inner voice, and the hardest of the three to pick out. Outer voices are simply louder to attention. That is exactly why people fall back on "it sounds sad": the note doing the work is the one the ear least wants to isolate.
The drill: same root, one finger
Take the two grips from the start of this chapter:

. Alternate them slowly, and listen to nothing but string 2. Everything else is a constant; the only thing changing in the whole sound is that one voice moving by a semitone. Learn what that motion sounds like and you have learned the difference.

, so the root is nailed down and the third is genuinely the only variable. Then close your eyes and let the finger land at random — you should be able to call it before the chord has finished ringing.

Do not stop there. Same-root pairs are a scaffold, and practised alone they teach your ear the absolute pitch of one note rather than the interval. Once the C pair is easy, change the root between attempts — the
will do that for you, and it is a noticeably harder exercise than it sounds.
Four chords, one of them minor
Now hear it in context. Four chords in C — A minor, F, C and G — all on strings 1-2-3, each one the nearest inversion to the last, and the whole loop living between fret 0 and fret 4.

props.caption: A minor, root position, strings 1-2-3 — the only minor chord in the loop.

The third has carried this entire chapter — one note, dropped one fret, in every grip on every set. The note that has not moved once is the fifth. Chapter 4 takes that one.
